title: Felix and the Lantern Bread
markdown:
In a tiny cottage tucked high in the Brackenhorn hills lived a young wizard named Felix. It was a cosy little place, walls of warm grey stone and a roof thatched with fluffy dried grasses. Sunlight liked to spill through the windows and make his spell books look as if they were whispering. Felix had eyes as bright as morning dew and a heart that loved new spells. He spent his days tracing zig-zag runes in the air, coaxing tiny sparks to dance, and trying to lift his favourite feather quill with his mind.

His best friend was Corvus, a sleek black crow with eyes like little shiny beads and a talent for finding the prettiest, smoothest pebbles. Corvus had been a gift from Aunt Willow, and he was still getting used to the bubbly smells of potions and the crackle of the hearth. He watched Felix practise, head tilted this way and that, and sometimes let out a cheerful caw that sounded remarkably like cheering.

One evening, as the moon climbed high, round and white like a giant pearl button, Felix remembered something important. Aunt Willow needed a shimmering moonpetal. The flower bloomed only when the moon was full, and he had promised to bring it before the sun peeked over the hills. He had been looking after it in a little pot by his window, where it soaked up the light.

“Oh, fiddlesticks,” Felix mumbled, patting his robe pockets. The soft wool felt sadly empty. “Where did I put that map?” A funny little flutter started in his tummy, like tiny wings. He did not want to disappoint Aunt Willow. She always gave the warmest hugs and the most delicious honey cakes. The thought of the fern-filled woods in dim light, a place that always seemed to whisper secrets he could not quite hear, made his hands feel a bit damp. He always worried he might get turned around, even on paths he thought he knew.

Corvus nudged Felix’s hand with his beak. Glossy feathers caught the moonlight like tiny dark jewels. “We’ll find it, won’t we?” His small bright eyes were full of courage. Felix managed a wobbly smile. The flutter calmed a little, replaced by a tiny spark of hope. “Yes, Corvus, we will,” he said, his voice a little steadier. He peeked under the soft rug, then behind the big comfy armchair. And there it was, tucked inside his favourite book of cloud shapes: the map, drawn on crinkly paper, with wobbly lines and little pictures.

With the shimmering moonpetal, petals like captured starlight, carefully tucked into his pouch, and Corvus perched on his shoulder, Felix opened the cottage door and stepped into the night. The ferns, so green and lush by day, now glowed with soft moonlight, their fronds unfurling like tiny welcoming hands. The air smelled of damp earth, sweet pine needles, and something faintly floral. The woods felt a little more rustly than usual, stretching out like a soft dark blanket dotted with stars peeking through the leaves. A twig snapped nearby. Damp chill on his skin. Sharp earthy scent of decaying leaves. A path split ahead, one way looking much like the other, and Felix nearly froze, feet rooted to the spot.

They followed the winding path, Felix squinting at the faint moonlight. Each shadow seemed to dance. The rustling leaves sounded like hushed conversations. Corvus cawed softly, pointing his beak this way and that, sharp eyes scanning the undergrowth. “Did you see that, Corvus? A little flicker of light.” Felix pointed to a tiny glow ahead, nestled amongst the ferns. As they got closer, it was not a single flicker but a whole row of warm yellow lights, bobbing gently.

Bustling around them, with a cheerful hum, was a little goblin with flour dusting his pointed hat and rosy cheeks that glowed in the lantern light. This was Cai Bumblesnuff, the baker, known throughout the Brackenhorn for his wonderfully light loaves and his wonderfully muddled way of speaking.

“Lanterns, you see,” Cai chirped, his voice as round and jolly as his buns. “Setting out my mountain lanterns, I am. Best light for finding your way to the juiciest berries, these are. And for my sunrise buns, oh yes. They need the first light, you understand.”

Felix blinked. “Mountain lanterns? But I’m looking for a special signal. My map had a picture of a lantern on it. It’s very important.”

Cai chuckled, his belly jiggling like a bowl of jelly. “Ah, yes. The most important lantern of all.” He held up a plump golden-brown loaf, shaped remarkably like a lantern, round top with a little loop handle, base tapering. The scent wafting up was warm and sweet, like honey and sunshine baked into bread, and Felix’s tummy rumbled just a little. Felix looked at the map again, then at the bread. The wobbly lines seemed to lead right to this very spot.

Felix realised, with a little sigh, that Cai wasn’t talking about a direction-finding lantern at all. The special lantern was a delicious warm bread. He really wanted to deliver the moonpetal to Aunt Willow before sunrise, and he thought she’d enjoy a tasty treat too. But when Felix asked if he could have the bread, Cai’s rosy cheeks drooped just a tiny bit. “Well, it’s my last one, you see,” he said, his voice losing some of its cheer. “I was saving it for old Mrs Crumbles, she’s ever so fond of them. But it’s very special, and takes my best spell to make it rise just right. It needs a smooth-stone spell starter to give it that extra bit of magic. Do you happen to have one?”

Felix’s heart sank, and the butterfly in his tummy did a quick somersault. He did have a very smooth grey river stone in his pocket. It was his favourite, perfectly rounded, and felt wonderfully cool and steady in his hand. He used it to begin his favourite beginner spells, the ones that made tiny sparks fizz. His hand hovered over it. He imagined the stone’s gentle rumble as he coaxed sparks from it, the faint scent of ozone it seemed to hold when a spell worked just right. Without that stone, his practice spells felt distant, like half-formed dreams. He pictured himself fumbling, his magic fizzing out before it even began.

He thought of Aunt Willow’s happy smile, and then of Mrs Crumbles, who always gave him warm cookies when he visited her garden. He knew, deep down, what he had to do. “I do,” Felix said, a little quiet. He opened his hand, and the river stone gleamed softly in the lantern light. He held it out to Cai. “I’ll trade you.”

Cai’s eyes widened, shining with surprise and gratitude. “Oh, my dear child. That’s a very generous trade. It means I won’t be able to practise my best new levitation spell this morning, as the stone helps me focus the energy just so, but Mrs Crumbles will be ever so pleased.”

Carrying the warm sweet-smelling bread, carefully wrapped in its leafy parcel, Felix and Corvus turned back towards the cottage. The ferns no longer seemed so mysterious; they rustled with a friendly whisper. The moonlight felt like a soft comforting blanket. Corvus hopped from Felix’s shoulder to the ground, then flew a little ahead, a dark shape against the moonlit sky. He would occasionally swoop back, a little black arrow against the soft glow. Felix hummed a little tune that had been tucked away in his mind. The bread’s warmth seeped into his hands through the leaf. He knew he would miss his smooth stone for a while, but the thought of Aunt Willow’s face when he gave her the moonpetal, and the warm bread, made him feel quite brave.

Soon they were back at their own cosy cottage, the little windows glowing from within. Aunt Willow was waiting, her face beaming, silver hair catching the light. When she saw the shimmering moonpetal, her eyes sparkled. “Oh, Felix, my dear. It’s perfect.” And then Felix shyly offered her the warm lantern bread. She hugged him tight, the scent of moonpetal and bread mingling. “What a wonderful surprise. And you found your way back all by yourself, didn’t you?”

Felix smiled, puffing out his chest just a little. He looked at Corvus, who hopped onto the table and pecked at a stray crumb. The Brackenhorn Range felt safe and familiar again, and the cottage smelled of dried herbs and honey cakes. He picked up his map, tracing a route that now seemed perfectly clear. He looked at Corvus, and with a calm assurance said, “This way, Corvus.” The stone was gone. The bread was warm. The moonpetal sat in Aunt Willow’s hands, which was how you knew a muddled baker’s lantern could still light the way home.
characters: Felix (young wizard of the Brackenhorn hills), Corvus (a sleek black crow)
author: StoryGen Community
